docs.text:
In principle, every acquisition can be structured into the following procedure: connect to the cards, load the sequence, set the acquisition parameters, run the acquisition and store the data.

Note

Usually, we would run an acquisition using the nexus service. This example serves as a quick reference to test the AcquisitionControl in a single Jupyter notebook or Python script.

docs.title: Acquisition control
docs.text:
In a first step, we import the AcquisitionControl and create an instance of it using the path to our device configuration. This loads and validates the device configuration and connects and configures both measurement cards.

Warning

When using an AcquisitionControl instance directly, you may want to create the instance before turning on your amplifiers (see Console hardware).

from console.spcm_control.acquisition_control import AcquisitionControl

acq = AcquisitionControl(configuration_file="device_config.yaml")

docs.title: Construct a sequence
docs.text:
Construct a PyPulseq sequence with the system limits of the console using one of the provided sequence constructors.

import console
from console.utilities.sequences import se_spectrum

seq = se_spectrum.constructor(echo_time=20e-3, rf_duration=200e-6, system=acq.get_sequence_system())
console.parameter.larmor_frequency = 2.0e6
console.parameter.num_averages = 1

docs.title: Set acquisition parameter
docs.text:
Parameters that can be adjusted and changed at runtime are kept in an AcquisitionParameter instance. On import, the package loads the last saved acquisition parameter state or creates a default state. Any change to the parameters is automatically synchronized with a JSON file on disk. This instance is created in the global scope so that it can be used across different scripts.

import console

console.parameter.larmor_frequency = 2.0e6
console.parameter.num_averages = 1

docs.title: Run acquisition
docs.text:
set_sequence uses the sequence and the acquisition parameter instance to calculate the waveforms that are replayed by the console (see sequence calculation for further details). Instead of the sequence instance, the path to a Pulseq sequence file can be used as well. After calculating the sequence waveforms, the sequence is executed using run(). The acquisition data is processed automatically and returned as an AcquisitionData instance.

acq.set_sequence(sequence=seq, parameter=console.parameter)
acq_data = acq.run()

docs.title: Save acquisition data
docs.text:
The acquisition data contains an RxData object for each ADC event that was acquired. One specific object can be selected from the list of acquired RxData objects. The acquired complex-valued signal is stored in the processed_data attribute. save() stores the AcquisitionData, the metadata and the sequence. Using save_ismrmrd(), the AcquisitionData can be stored in ISMRMRD format. To close the card connection, delete the AcquisitionControl instance.

rx_data = acq_data.receive_data[0]           # first ADC event of the first average
signal = rx_data.processed_data              # complex, shape (channels, samples)
acq_data.add_info({"note": "first acquisition"})
acq_data.save()                              # store HDF5, meta.json and sequence.seq
acq_data.save_ismrmrd()                      # ISMRMRD file

# Disconnect from the cards
del acq

Instead of manually creating and deleting the AcquisitionControl in the experiment script, the cards can be operated by a persistent service (see Acquisition service). Complete experiments are given in the Examples.

docs.title: Hardware setup
docs.text:
This page describes how to set up the console hardware with one arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) module and one digitizer module. The interaction of the console workstation with the other components of the MRI system is explained in the System overview.

Supported cards

The software was developed with and for measurement cards from Spectrum Instrumentation. Specifically for the arbitrary waveform generator module M2p.6546-x4 and the digitizer module M2p.5933-x4. We expect other modules from the M2p family to work with the framework as well, but we haven't tested this yet.

One transmit and one receive card

So far, the software is designed for exactly one transmit and one receive card.

Synchronization

The transmit and receive cards are synchronized by a wired connection between the cards. Synchronization via the Star-Hub module is not supported yet. This is work in progress and will be added later.

docs.title: Measurement cards and driver
docs.text:
Disclaimer

Installing, wiring and operating the measurement cards and the connected MRI hardware is at your own risk. The developers of this software framework assume no responsibility or liability for any damage to the measurement cards, the computer system hosting the measurement cards or other hardware resulting from installation, wiring or use. Always follow the safety and installation instructions in the official Spectrum Instrumentation manuals [6].

  1. Install the cards and the driver as described in the hardware manual of each card, available from the Spectrum Instrumentation download area (e.g. the M2p.65xx manual and the M2p.59xx manual). The relevant chapters are Safety Instructions, Hardware Installation and Software Driver Installation and Driver Update.
  2. Install the Spectrum Control Center (section Control Center in the driver installation chapter of the manual) and use it to verify that both cards are detected.
  3. Note the device paths of both cards (/dev/spcm0, /dev/spcm1, ...). They are required for the device configuration.

docs.title: Connection plan
docs.text: The connector names below are those printed on the card brackets. Analog channels, clock input and trigger input use SMB connectors, the multi-purpose lines X0–X3 use MMCX connectors, so some connections require adapter cables (e.g. MMCX to SMB). The complete port assignment of both cards, including the unused ports, is listed in Console hardware.

docs.title: Card synchronization
docs.text:
For the card synchronization shorter adapter cables are required (10-20 cm, depending on the PCIe slot positions). This includes MMCX to SMB for the clock synchronization and two MMCX to MMCX cables.

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear"}}}%%
flowchart LR
    subgraph TX["AWG / TX card"]
        TXCLK["<b>Clk In</b><br/><i>SMB</i>"]
        TXX1["<b>X1</b><br/><i>MMCX</i>"]
        TXX2["<b>X2</b><br/><i>MMCX</i>"]
    end
    subgraph RX["Digitizer / RX card"]
        RXX0["<b>X0/CO</b><br/><i>MMCX</i>"]
        RXX1["<b>X1</b><br/><i>MMCX</i>"]
        RXX2["<b>X2</b><br/><i>MMCX</i>"]
    end
    %% All links run from TX to RX to keep the cards side by side,
    %% the clock link hides its arrowhead at RX so that it points from RX to TX
    TXCLK <-->|"Clock"| RXX0
    TXX1 -->|"ADC gate"| RXX1
    TXX2 -->|"Phase reference"| RXX2
    linkStyle 0 marker-end:none
  • Clock: The transmit card is configured to run on an external clock which is provided by the receive card, whereby both cards sample synchronously. The sampling rates of both cards in the device configuration must therefore be identical.
  • ADC gate: The transmit card outputs a digital gate signal on X1 that is high during each ADC event of the sequence. The receive card uses X1 as logic trigger input and records exactly the gated samples.
  • Phase reference: The transmit card outputs a square wave on X2, which the receive card samples together with the MR signal. It is used to correct the phase of each acquisition (see Phase reference).

docs.title: MRI system
docs.text:
Card Port Port type Connection to Signal AWG 0 SMB RFPA input RF waveforms calculated from the Pulseq sequence AWG X3 MMCX RFPA unblanking Digital RF unblanking signal (5 V high) AWG 1–3 SMB GPA inputs Gradient waveforms of the three gradient axes calculated from the Pulseq sequence Digitizer 0 SMB Preamplifier output Received and preamplified MR signal

The assignment of the gradient outputs on the console side to the gradient power amplifier and the respective gradient coils is fixed. However, the mapping from the Pulseq gradient channels (x, y, z) to the console outputs can be adjusted using the acquisition parameter channel_assignment (default: x → 1, y → 2, z → 3).

With an IO expansion module on the transmit card, the ADC gate and the unblanking signal are additionally available on X12 and X13.

docs.title: Hardware configuration
docs.text:
Before starting with the installation of the nexus-console, you should collect all required hardware parameters of your specific setup:

  • The device paths of the measurement cards, obtained, for instance, from the spcmcontrol software.
  • The maximum amplitude per channel (for the AWG and digitizer modules). The maximum output amplitude should be compatible with the maximum input ratings of the amplifiers (RFPA and GPA).

  • The load impedance of each AWG output (50 Ω or high impedance).

    Output voltage doubles into high-impedance loads

    The AWG outputs have a 50 Ω series termination and the programmed amplitude refers to a 50 Ω load. If an output drives a high-impedance load instead, the output voltage is double the programmed value. Usually, the RF line (AWG channel 0) is connected to the 50 Ω input of the RFPA, while the gradient lines (AWG channels 1–3) are connected to high-impedance GPA inputs. The console compensates for the doubling based on the device configuration.

  • If you use more than one receive channel, enable the corresponding channels and set the termination per channel.

  • The GPA gain in A/V.
  • The efficiency of each of your gradient channels in T/m/A. The gradient efficiency and the GPA gain determine whether the sequence is replayed correctly.

Continue with the Installation of the software.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page describes the installation of the console software. It assumes that the hardware is set up as described in Hardware setup.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.13
  • Spectrum Instrumentation driver for the measurement cards

docs.title: Python package
docs.text:
Install the package into a virtual environment (venv or conda):

pip install nexus-console

For development, clone the repository and install it in editable mode with the optional dependency groups:

git clone https://github.com/schote/nexus-console.git
cd nexus-console
pip install -e ".[test,lint,dev]"
Extra Content test pytest and coverage lint ruff, mypy dev Profiling and notebook tools docs-mkdocs Documentation build

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Verify the installation by running the following command.

nexus --help

If the installation was successful, you should see the help context of the command you can start the nexus-service with.

docs.title: Device configuration
docs.text: Before you can start executing sequences, you need to create a device configuration file. Copy the example examples/example_device_config.yaml which serves as a template and adapt it to your hardware, including the device paths and the termination noted during the hardware setup. The keys are explained in Device configuration. Continue with the first acquisition.

docs.title: Acquisition service
docs.text: The nexus command starts a persistent acquisition service. It connects to the measurement cards once and keeps the connection open, while experiment scripts and notebooks connect to the service as clients to run acquisitions.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
In the first acquisition, the experiment script creates AcquisitionControl itself, so the cards are connected and disconnected with every script run or kernel restart. Running the cards in a separate service has several advantages:

  • Less overhead: every connection resets and configures the cards (clock, sampling rate, channels, digital outputs) and starts the processing workers. With the service, this setup is done once per session instead of with every script run.
  • Robustness: a crashing script or a restarted notebook kernel does not affect the card connection.
  • Separation: hardware control runs in its own process, independent of the environment used for sequence design, reconstruction and plotting.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C["Experiment script<br/>or notebook"]
    subgraph S["nexus service"]
        A["AcquisitionControl"]
    end
    H["TX / RX cards"]

    C -- "sequence +<br/>parameters" ---> A
    A -- "AcquisitionData" ---> C
    A <--> H

The service creates a single AcquisitionControl instance and serves it via AcquisitionControlManager (nexus_service.acquisition_manager), a Python multiprocessing manager. Clients receive a proxy object which behaves like a local AcquisitionControl: method calls such as set_sequence and run are executed in the service process, their arguments are sent to the service and the resulting AcquisitionData is returned to the client.

Service and clients communicate through a unix domain socket on the workstation. The service is not reachable over the network; to use the console from another computer, log in via SSH and run the client there.

docs.title: Starting the service
docs.text:
Start the service in a separate terminal on the computer with the measurement cards:

nexus -d path/to/device_config.yaml

The service asks for confirmation that all amplifiers are switched off, connects the cards and then waits for clients.

Option Description Default -d, --device_config Device configuration file (required) -l, --log_dir Directory of the log file <date>_nexus.log ~/nexus-console -n, --no-verify Skip the amplifier confirmation prompt

Stop the service with Ctrl+C, which disconnects the cards.

To start the service automatically at system boot, run it as a systemd unit under a dedicated account instead, see Service deployment.

docs.title: Running an acquisition
docs.text:
Clients resolve the socket and the authentication key from the runtime directory, so the manager is constructed without arguments. The remote instance is accessed as manager.acquisition:

import console
from nexus_service.acquisition_manager import AcquisitionControlManager
from console.utilities.sequences import se_spectrum

console.parameter.larmor_frequency = 2.0e6

with AcquisitionControlManager() as manager:
    system = manager.acquisition.get_sequence_system()
    seq = se_spectrum.constructor(echo_time=20e-3, rf_duration=200e-6, system=system)

    manager.acquisition.set_sequence(sequence=seq, parameter=console.parameter)
    acq_data = manager.acquisition.run()

acq_data.save()

The client uses the same API as a local AcquisitionControl, so existing scripts only need to replace the instantiation.

One client at a time

All clients share a single AcquisitionControl instance, and the service does not serialize access to it. Each client connection is handled in its own thread, so calls of different clients run concurrently: a set_sequence of a second client can replace the sequence of the first one before its run, and two simultaneous run calls access the cards at the same time. Coordinate the use of the console so that only one client runs acquisitions at a time.

If the service is not running, constructing or entering the manager raises a NexusNotRunningError, a ConnectionError whose message explains how to start the service.

A complete client example is given in Remote acquisition.

docs.title: Acquisition data
docs.text: The service does not store acquisition data. manager.acquisition.run() returns the AcquisitionData object to the client, and save() and save_ismrmrd() run in the client process, i.e. under the account which called them. Without a user_path, the data is written to ~/nexus-console/<date>-session of that account; with user_path, the session folder is created in the given directory.

docs.title: Runtime directory
docs.text:
Service and clients exchange the connection details through a runtime directory. When the service is started by hand, this is <tempdir>/nexus (a systemd unit uses /run/nexus, see Service deployment). The environment variable NEXUS_RUNTIME_DIR overrides the location, e.g. to isolate tests from a running service.

File Description nexus.sock Unix domain socket of the service, accessible by every account authkey Authentication key, generated at every service start and readable by every account

The directory is created with mode 1777, the same permissions that /tmp uses. Every account on the workstation can read the key and connect to the socket, while the sticky bit allows only the owner of a file to delete or rename it, so no account can remove the socket or the key of another. If the directory is a symbolic link or has different permissions, e.g. because another account created it beforehand, the service and the clients refuse to use it.

Note that /tmp is periodically cleaned by the system, and that leftovers of another account can only be removed by that account or root.

The authentication key is not a secret

The key only ensures that clients connect to the currently running service, not to one from a previous run. It does not protect against other users of the workstation: any client holding the key can make the service execute code on its behalf, and the measurement cards are world-accessible character devices. Run the service under an ordinary operator account, never as root.

Both files are removed when the service shuts down. If the service is killed without being able to clean up, the socket file remains; the next service start detects that nothing is listening behind it and removes it. A second service instance started while the first one is still running aborts with an error instead of interfering with the running acquisition.

Windows

Windows has neither unix domain sockets nor POSIX permissions. There, the service listens on a named pipe named after the socket path, \\.\pipe\<runtime directory>/nexus.sock, which vanishes with the service, and the runtime directory is <tempdir>\nexus, which is private to the account. Windows only grants the account which started the service write access to the pipe, so only this account can connect to it.

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text: An acquisition is executed by AcquisitionControl.run after the sequence has been calculated by set_sequence. The AWG replays the calculated sequence while the digitizer records one gate per ADC event. Each average is a complete replay of the sequence.

docs.title: Sequence of operations
docs.text:
---
config:
  fontFamily: Inter, sans-serif
  # Larger text; narrower participants and margins keep the diagram from being scaled down
  sequence:
    actorFontSize: 18
    messageFontSize: 18
    noteFontSize: 18
    width: 120
    actorMargin: 30
  # Replaces Material's sequence diagram styles for this diagram: participants coloured like the
  # other diagrams (host software blue, measurement cards orange), lifelines and loop borders neutral.
  # Mermaid drops a themeCSS that contains ">", hence descendant instead of child selectors.
  themeCSS: |
    .actor { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-actor-bg-color); stroke: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-actor-border-color) }
    text.actor tspan { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-actor-fg-color); font-family: var(--md-mermaid-font-family) }
    rect.actor[name=AC], rect.actor[name=TX], rect.actor[name=RX], rect.actor[name=P] { fill: #2f6bff22; stroke: #2f6bff }
    rect.actor[name=AWG], rect.actor[name=DIG] { fill: #e67e2222; stroke: #e67e22 }
    .actor-line { stroke: var(--md-default-fg-color) }
    .messageLine0, .messageLine1 { stroke: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-message-line-color) }
    .messageText { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-message-fg-color); stroke: none; font-family: var(--md-mermaid-font-family) !important }
    #arrowhead path { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-message-line-color); stroke: none }
    .loopLine { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-loop-bg-color); stroke: var(--md-default-fg-color--light) }
    .loopText, .loopText tspan { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-loop-fg-color); stroke: none; font-family: var(--md-mermaid-font-family) !important }
    .labelBox { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-label-bg-color); stroke: none }
    .sequenceNumber { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-number-fg-color) }
    defs #sequencenumber { fill: var(--md-mermaid-sequence-number-bg-color) !important }
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant AC as AcquisitionControl
    participant TX as TxCard
    participant RX as RxCard
    participant P as RxProcessor
    participant AWG
    participant DIG as Digitizer

    AC->>TX: Set gradient offsets
    AC->>RX: Start operation
    RX->>DIG: Start card, wait for ADC gates
    RX-->>AC: Ready
    AC->>TX: Start operation
    TX->>AWG: Fill ring buffer and start replay
    par AWG thread
        loop Until the replay buffer is transferred
            AWG-->>TX: Chunk consumed
            TX->>AWG: Refill chunk
        end
    and Digitizer thread
        loop For each ADC event
            AWG->>DIG: ADC gate and phase reference
            DIG->>RX: Timestamps and gate data
            RX->>P: Submit RxData
        end
    and Main thread
        AC->>AC: Wait for all gates
    end
    AC->>TX: Stop operation
    AC->>RX: Stop operation
    AC->>TX: Reset gradient offsets
    AC->>P: Collect processed RxData

Steps 2–14 are executed once per average; the next average starts after averaging_delay. Averages are not summed, each RxData carries its average_index.

Steps Description 1, 15 The gradient offsets of the acquisition parameters are written to the offset registers of AWG channels 1–3 before the first average and reset to zero after the last. 2–5 The digitizer is started first and waits for the first ADC gate. As soon as its thread is ready, the AWG is started; it uses a software trigger, so the replay begins immediately. 6–8 The AWG replays the sequence while the TX thread refills the ring buffer (see AWG: FIFO streaming). 9–11 The ADC gates and the phase reference embedded in the replay buffer (see Sequence calculation) trigger the gated recording of the digitizer (see Digitizer: gated recording). Each gate is submitted for processing while the acquisition continues (see Postprocessing). 12 The main thread polls the number of received gates every 100 ms and reports the progress to the optional progress_callback. The average ends when all gates are received, or after a timeout of 5 s plus the sequence duration. 13, 14 Both cards are stopped as soon as the last gate is received, so blocks after the last ADC event (e.g. a final TR delay) are not necessarily played out completely. 16 The processed RxData of all averages are collected in order.

docs.title: AWG: FIFO streaming mode
docs.text:
Parameter Value Ring buffer Page-aligned DMA buffer in host memory; size of the replay buffer rounded up to whole chunks, at most 1 GiB Chunk size Notify size of the DMA transfer: 1/16 of the ring buffer, at least 4 KiB. The driver signals each consumed chunk. Start (step 6) The ring buffer is filled completely before the card is started, so sequences that fit into it are transferred at once Refill (steps 7–8) One chunk of the replay buffer each time the card has consumed one End The last chunk is zero-padded, so all outputs return to 0 V

Sequences longer than the on-board memory are replayed without interruption as long as the host transfers the data faster than the card replays them (see Console hardware).

docs.title: Digitizer: gated recording mode
docs.text: Parameter Value Trigger (step 9) Rising edge of the ADC gate at X1; the card records while the gate is high Timestamps (step 10) Start and end of each gate; their difference gives the number of samples of the gate Data buffer (step 10) 1 GiB DMA ring buffer in host memory, notify size 4 KiB; the wrap-around at the end of the buffer is handled during readout Pre-trigger 8 samples per gate, removed during readout Phase reference (step 11) Bit 15 of channel 0 during the first ≤ 1000 samples of the gate; stored separately in RxData and removed from the analog data

docs.title: Device configuration
docs.text:
The device configuration describes the hardware of the MRI system: the measurement cards, the amplifiers, the gradient coils and the system limits. It is read from a YAML file when AcquisitionControl is created and remains fixed for the session. Parameters that change between measurements, such as the Larmor frequency, are passed with every sequence as AcquisitionParameter.

flowchart LR
    Y(["YAML file"]) -->|"load_nexus_config"| N["NexusConfiguration"]
    N -->|"TxConfiguration"| T["TxCard"]
    N -->|"RxConfiguration"| R["RxCard"]
    N -->|"RxConfiguration"| P["RxProcessor"]
    N -->|"TxConfiguration,<br/>SystemLimits"| S["SequenceProvider"]
    N -->|"complete copy"| D["AcquisitionData"]

    classDef sw fill:#2f6bff22,stroke:#2f6bff,stroke-width:1.5px
    classDef iface fill:#8e44ad22,stroke:#8e44ad,stroke-width:1.5px
    class N,T,R,P,S,D sw
    class Y iface

The file is validated by NexusConfiguration and consists of the three sections described below. Unknown keys are ignored. A copy of the complete configuration is stored with every acquisition in meta["device_configuration"].

docs.title: TxConfiguration
docs.text:
Transmit card (AWG), validated by TxConfiguration. channel_max_amplitude and channel_filter_type have four entries in the order [RF, gradient 1, gradient 2, gradient 3]; gradient_efficiency and gpa_gain have three entries, one per physical gradient channel.

Attribute Unit Description device_path – Device path of the transmit card, e.g. /dev/spcm1 sampling_rate MHz Sampling rate as integer; must equal RxConfiguration.sampling_rate, as the transmit card runs on the clock of the receive card (not checked by the software) channel_max_amplitude mV Output range per channel, 1–6000 mV into 50 Ω channel_filter_type – Output filter setting per channel, 0–3 (see card manual) rf_terminated_50ohm – true if the RF output is terminated into 50 Ω, false for high impedance (the output voltage doubles) gradients_terminated_50ohm – true if the gradient outputs are terminated into 50 Ω, false for high impedance (the output voltage doubles) gradient_efficiency T/m/A Gradient coil efficiency per physical gradient channel gpa_gain A/V Transconductance of the gradient power amplifier per physical gradient channel rf_to_mvolt mV/Hz Conversion of the PyPulseq RF amplitude to the output voltage rf_gain_lut_path – Optional, default none. Path to a lookup table for the linearization of the RF power amplifier (.npy, 65536 int16 values)

docs.title: RxConfiguration
docs.text:
Receive card (digitizer), validated by RxConfiguration. All channel lists must have max_available_channels entries. As the receive card setup expects 8 entries per list, max_available_channels must currently be 8, also for cards with fewer channels.

Attribute Unit Description device_path – Device path of the receive card, e.g. /dev/spcm0 sampling_rate MHz Sampling rate as integer; the receive card is the clock master and provides this clock to the transmit card max_available_channels – Number of input channels of the card and length of all channel lists (8 for the M2p.5933-x4) channel_enable – Enable flag per channel; 1, 2, 4 or 8 channels must be enabled channel_max_amplitude mV Input range per channel: 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 or 10000 channel_terminated_50ohm – Input termination per channel, true for 50 Ω, false for high impedance num_processing_workers – Optional, default 1. Number of worker processes for the parallel processing of the receive data; 0 processes the data in the main process after the acquisition

docs.title: SystemLimits
docs.text:
Limits of the MR system, validated by SystemLimits and passed to PyPulseq as Opts (AcquisitionControl.get_sequence_system()). max_grad, max_slew, block_duration_raster, grad_raster_time and adc_raster_time must be positive, all other values must not be negative. Numbers in exponent notation need a decimal point, e.g. 20.e-6: YAML reads 20e-6 as a string, which the model rejects.

Attribute Unit Description max_grad Hz/m Maximum gradient amplitude max_slew Hz/m/s Maximum gradient slew rate rf_dead_time s Dead time before an RF pulse; the RF unblanking signal is set this time before the pulse rf_ringdown_time s Ring-down time after an RF pulse adc_dead_time s Dead time around an ADC event; the ADC gate is extended by this time on both sides block_duration_raster s Raster time of block durations rf_raster_time s Raster time of RF waveforms grad_raster_time s Raster time of gradient waveforms adc_raster_time s Raster time of ADC dwell times B0 T Optional, default 0.05. Static magnetic field strength

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The example configuration of the repository must be adapted to the target system.

examples/example_device_config.yaml
# ========================================
# Configuration file for the Nexus-console
# ========================================

# NOTE: This is just an example, parameters need to be adjusted for individual system

# >> TX DEVICE: M2p.6546-x4 -> /dev/spcm1 (AWG)
# Total number of (analog) transmit channels: 4
TxConfiguration:
  # Could be extended to a list
  device_path: "/dev/spcm1"
  # Number of channels
  max_available_channels: 4
  # Device sampling rate in MHz
  sampling_rate: 20
  # Max. output amplitude per channel in mV
  channel_max_amplitude: [200, 6000, 6000, 6000]
  # Filter configuration of each transmit channel
  channel_filter_type: [0, 2, 2, 2]
  # Configure if RF/gradients are terminated into 50 ohm impedance (true == 50 ohm)
  rf_terminated_50ohm: True
  gradients_terminated_50ohm: False
  # Calculate grad_to_volt per gradient channel:
  # Gradient efficiency in T/m/A
  gradient_efficiency: [0.37e-3, 0.451e-3, 0.4e-3]
  # Gradient power amplifier in A/V
  gpa_gain: [7.10, 7.10, 7.10]
  # Scales RF in Hz (pulseq) to mV
  rf_to_mvolt: 5.e-3
  # rf_gain_lut_path: "/path/to/lut.npy"


# >> RX DEVICE: M2p.5933-x4 -> /dev/spcm0 (Digitizer)
# Total number of receive channels: 8
RxConfiguration:
  # Could be extended to a list
  device_path: "/dev/spcm0"
  # Number of channels
  max_available_channels: 8
  # Device sampling rate in MHz
  sampling_rate: 20
  # Enable the receive channels
  channel_enable: [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
  # Set the max. amplitude per channel in mV, list length must at least match the number of enabled channels
  channel_max_amplitude: [200, 200, 200, 200, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000]
  # Configure which channels are terminated into 50 ohm impedance (true == 50 ohm), list length must at least match the number of enabled channels
  channel_terminated_50ohm: [True, True, True, True, False, False, False, False]

SystemLimits:
  # Maximum gradient amplitude in Hz/m (PyPulseq system stores this unit)
  max_grad: 1703040.0 # equals 40 mT/m
  # Maximum slew rate in Hz/m/s (PyPulseq system stores this unit)
  max_slew: 2128800000.0 # equals 100 T/m/s
  # Dead time at the beginning of RF event in s, covered by rf_delay
  rf_dead_time: 20.e-6
  # Time delay at the end of an RF event in s
  rf_ringdown_time: 30.e-6
  # Time delay at the beginning of an ADC event in s
  adc_dead_time: 0.
  # Raster time for block durations
  block_duration_raster: 1.e-6
  # Raster time for RF pulses.
  rf_raster_time: 1.e-6
  # Raster time for gradient waveforms.
  grad_raster_time: 1.e-6
  # Raster time for ADC readout.
  adc_raster_time: 1.e-6

docs.title: Console hardware
docs.text:
The Nexus console uses PCIe measurement cards from Spectrum Instrumentation, installed in a high-performance workstation. This page summarizes the hardware requirements of the console software and the considerations behind the choice of components. The installation is described in Hardware setup.

Development setup

The components and the port assignment on this page describe the setup that was used for the development of the console [1]. Other workstations and other cards of the same families might work as well, but have not been tested.

docs.title: Workstation
docs.text:
The workstation hosts both measurement cards. In the current implementation, the complete sequence is calculated and stored in host memory before execution. During the acquisition, the workstation streams the waveforms to the AWG, reads the gated receive data from the digitizer and processes them in parallel. The considerations below assume a sampling rate of 20 MHz, as used in the development setup.

Planned improvements

Several improvements are planned for future versions. One is to calculate the sequence at runtime, so that the memory requirement no longer scales with the sequence duration. In turn, sequence calculation, streaming and receive processing will run in parallel, which requires more CPU cores and a sequence calculation that is faster than real time. In addition, the measurement cards can transfer data directly to a GPU using SCAPP. Future versions of the Nexus console might therefore benefit from an on-board GPU.

Component Development setup Reasoning PCIe Supermicro X12SPL-F, 7 slots Each card requires one slot with 4 lanes (-x4). The required transfer rates of 160 MB/s for the AWG and 40 MB/s per enabled receive channel (while the gate is open) are well below the card interface rate of about 700 MB/s. The remaining slots are available for a GPU, NVMe storage or additional cards. AWG Spectrum M2p.6546-x4 with IO expansion module Four 16-bit channels on one card allow RF and the three gradients to be replayed sample-synchronously from a single buffer. The output range of ±6 V into 50 Ω (±12 V into high impedance) drives the RFPA and GPA inputs directly. 40 MS/s provide sufficient oversampling at the Larmor frequency of the development setup (~2 MHz). Bit 15 of channels 1–3 drives the synchronous digital outputs X1–X3, so the ADC gate, phase reference and RF unblanking are generated together with the waveforms, without separate timing hardware. Digitizer Spectrum M2p.5933-x4 Eight 16-bit channels at 40 MS/s record the MR signal and additional sensors, e.g. EMI sensing coils. The MR signal is sampled directly and demodulated digitally on the host, so no analog receive chain beyond the preamplifier is needed. The synchronously sampled digital input X2 provides a phase reference that corrects the phase of each gate for the jitter of the gate detection. RAM 256 GB The unrolled sequence requires 4 channels × 2 bytes (int16) per sampling clock, i.e. 160 MB per second or 9.6 GB per minute of sequence. Averages replay the same buffer and need no additional memory. Allowing about 16 GB for the operating system, the Python processes and the two 1 GiB DMA buffers, 256 GB are sufficient for sequences of roughly 25 minutes. The processed receive data are small in comparison (16 bytes per complex sample and channel, e.g. 34 MB for 128 × 128 × 128 samples), unless the raw data are kept with run(store_unprocessed=True). CPU Intel Xeon Gold 6312U, 24 cores The acquisition process runs the TX streaming and RX readout threads, which must keep up with the cards in real time, while num_processing_workers worker processes demodulate and decimate the gates in parallel. Therefore, at least 2 + num_processing_workers cores should be available, plus one for the acquisition service. The sequence calculation currently runs in a single process, so single-core performance determines the duration of set_sequence. Future parallelization of the sequence calculation or processing may require additional cores. Storage NVMe SSD Data are written to disk after the acquisition, so storage speed does not affect the acquisition itself. GPU Optional Not yet required by the Nexus console, but useful for AI-based processing on the console workstation. Future versions might stream the acquired data directly to the GPU for faster processing. Operating system AlmaLinux 9.3, Windows 10 Both are supported by the Spectrum driver (development setup: kernel driver M2p 2.17 build 17916, library 6.05 build 21120).

Card requirements of the software

The current Nexus console implementation supports exactly one transmit and one receive card. On connection, the software checks that the transmit card belongs to the M2p.65xx family (AWG) and the receive card to the M2p.59xx family (digitizer). The cards are synchronized by cables, as described in Hardware setup, and share the clock provided by the digitizer module. Both cards must therefore run at the same sampling rate. Synchronization via a Star-Hub might be added in the future.

docs.text: The multi-purpose lines X0–X3 are pulled high while the software opens the connection to the cards (issue #54). As X3 drives the RFPA unblanking input, this can affect the amplifier, e.g. if it has a safety mechanism that is triggered by an overly long gate signal.

docs.title: System overview

The Nexus console is an open source software framework to operate PCIe measurement cards from Spectrum Instrumentation in a high performance computer system. Pulse sequences are defined in the open Pulseq format [2], converted directly into sampled waveforms on the host computer and streamed to the transmit card. Receive data are recorded in a gated mode, processed on the host and exported in the ISMRMRD format [4]. docs.text:
The nexus console builds on the following interfaces which can be understood as the input and output of the system.

Interface Description Reference Pulseq Open, vendor-independent sequence format. Sequences are created with (Py-)Pulseq and passed to the console as a PyPulseq Sequence object or a .seq file. docs.title: Software
docs.text:
The table gives and overview of the most important software modules implemented within the Nexus console.

It serves a single AcquisitionControl instance such that clients receive a proxy that behaves like a local AcquisitionControl. Acquisition service, Service deployment AcquisitionControl Loads the device configuration, creates the sequence provider, both cards and the processing pool. It controls the sequence calculation and execution. Device configuration AcquisitionParameter Runtime parameters of an acquisition, e.g. Larmor frequency, gradient offsets, etc. Acquisition SequenceProvider Subclass of the PyPulseq Sequence that calculates the sequence into the sampled transmit waveforms. Sequence calculation UnrolledSequence The resulting calculated sequence composed of the RF and gradients waveforms and digital control signals. It also includes the RxData templates and the parameters used for the scaling the waveforms. Sequence calculation TxCard Sets up the AWG module and streams the sequence waveform to the AWG module. Acquisition RxCard Sets up the digitizer and performs the gated recording. Acquisition RxData Data of one ADC event containing meta information, processing parameters, the raw samples and the processed data. Postprocessing RxProcessor Pool of worker processes that performs the postprocessing during the acquisition. Postprocessing, [5] AcquisitionData Result container with the receive data, the sequence, the device configuration and the acquisition parameters. Acquisition, [4] spcm_core Low-level Python bindings of the Spectrum driver, provided by Spectrum Instrumentation as a python package. spcm-core Spectrum driver Vendor driver library and kernel module to configure the measurement card operations and transfer the data between host memory and the cards. docs.text:
The hardware components mentioned in the diagram above are briefly explained below and summarize a minimal set needed to do MRI. The table lists example components where most of them are open source, which could be used to build a working MRI system.

Composition of the Hardware

This documentation focusses on the Nexus console. It does not address the composition of an MRI system. For additional information or documentation about how to build the hardware components listed below visit the OSI² GitLab.

Component Description Example AWG Arbitrary waveform generator. Outputs the RF and gradient waveforms together with the digital control signals for synchronisation and RF unblanking. M2p.5933-x4 Digitizer Records the MR signal in gates triggered by the AWG. M2p.6546-x4 Gradient power amplifier (GPA) Converts the gradient waveforms into coil currents. TU Delft GA2 Gradient coils Generate the gradient fields for spatial encoding. 32cm Gradient Insert RF power amplifier (RFPA) Amplifies the RF waveform; enabled by the unblanking signal around each RF pulse. RFPA-Shoebox T/R switch Routes the RFPA output to the RF coil during transmission and the coil signal to the preamplifier during reception, protecting the receive chain. Passive TR Switch RF coil Antenna handling the transmission of RF energy and the reception of the MR signal (usually we use the same coil for transmit and receive). docs.title: Postprocessing
docs.text:
Each ADC gate recorded by the digitizer is converted from raw ADC values into a complex baseband signal at the dwell time of the PyPulseq ADC event. The processing runs in parallel to the acquisition: the RX thread submits every gate as an RxData object to the RxProcessor, a pool of num_processing_workers worker processes that is started once when AcquisitionControl is created. The raw samples are passed to the workers via shared memory. With num_processing_workers: 0, all gates are processed in the main process after the acquisition. After processing, the raw samples are discarded unless run(store_unprocessed=True) is used.

    C --> Dec["Decimation"]
    Dec --> O["Processed data<br/>(complex float)"]

docs.title: Processing steps
docs.text:
The steps are implemented in RxData.process_data and applied to each receive channel of a gate:

Step Operation Scaling The int16 values are converted to mV with the input range of the channel: value × channel_max_amplitude / 32768. Demodulation The signal is multiplied by \(e^{-j 2\pi f_\text{d} t}\), with the demodulation frequency \(f_\text{d}\) = Larmor frequency + frequency offset of the ADC event and the time \(t\) from the start of the gate. Phase correction The phase measured with the phase reference (see below) is removed, and the phase offset of the ADC event is applied, i.e. the signal is multiplied by \(e^{j \varphi_\text{ADC}}\). Decimation The signal is low-pass filtered and down-sampled to the dwell time of the ADC event (see Decimation filters). The decimation factor is the ratio of the ADC dwell time and the sampling interval of the digitizer. The result is multiplied by 2, which compensates the signal component at \(-2 f_\text{d}\) that is removed by the low-pass filter.

The processed data of a gate contain num_samples + 2 × num_samples_discard complex samples per receive channel, i.e. the ADC samples plus the samples of the gate extension on both sides (see ADC events).

docs.title: Phase reference
docs.text:
The gate detection of the digitizer is not phase-locked to the replay of the AWG, so the phase of the demodulated signal would vary from gate to gate. To correct this, the digitizer samples the phase reference, a 1.095 MHz square wave that the AWG outputs at the start of each gate (see Sequence calculation). The phase of the reference is determined by demodulating the first ≤ 1000 reference samples at \(f_\text{ref}\) = 1.095 MHz and summing them. The phase at \(f_\text{ref}\) corresponds to a time offset, which is converted to the phase at the demodulation frequency:

\[ \varphi_\text{ref} = \arg\left( \sum r(t)\, e^{-j 2\pi f_\text{ref} t} \right) \cdot \frac{f_\text{d}}{f_\text{ref}} \]

The signal of the gate is then multiplied by \(e^{-j \varphi_\text{ref}}\).

docs.title: Decimation filters
docs.text:
The filter is selected by AcquisitionParameter.ddc_method (DDCMethod). The decimation factor must be greater than 1.

Method Implementation FIR (default) scipy.signal.decimate with an FIR anti-aliasing filter CIC Five-stage cascaded integrator-comb filter [5] that decimates by about half the decimation factor, followed by an FIR decimation by 2 AVG Strided convolution with a windowed kernel that spans 8 decimated samples

docs.text: Object Content RxData One ADC event of one average: metadata of the event, PyPulseq labels, time stamp of the gate, processed_data (complex, shape (channels, samples)) and optionally raw_data AcquisitionData Result of AcquisitionControl.run: flat list of all RxData, ordered by average and then by ADC event, the sequence, the acquisition parameters and metadata including the device configuration

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
All files of an acquisition are written to the folder <session>/<acquisition id>/. The session folder is <home>/nexus-console/<YYYY-MM-DD>-session by default; the acquisition id consists of date, time and sequence name, e.g. 2026-10-29-143012-se_spectrum.

Method Output AcquisitionData.save() rx_data.h5: metadata and one group per RxData with its metadata, processed_data and, if kept, raw_data meta.json: software version, date and time, acquisition id, acquisition parameters, sequence name, duration and definitions, device configuration and additional information from add_info sequence.seq: the PyPulseq sequence <key>.npy: additional arrays added with add_data AcquisitionData.save_ismrmrd() data.mrd in ISMRMRD format [4], see below

An existing meta.json or sequence.seq is only overwritten with save(overwrite=True).

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
The directions are given in the patient coordinate system (LPS), assuming a patient in supine, head-first position and the following orientation of the physical gradient channels:

Physical channel Patient direction LPS vector 1 Inferior → superior (0, 0, 1) 2 Posterior → anterior (0, −1, 0) 3 Right → left (1, 0, 0)

read_dir, phase_dir and slice_dir are the vectors of the physical channels assigned to the logical axes x, y and z by channel_assignment. They are identical for all acquisitions.

docs.title: Trajectory
docs.text: The k-space trajectory of all ADC samples is calculated from the sequence with PyPulseq (calculate_kspace). Only the axes whose values are non-zero for all samples are exported. The acquisitions take consecutive sections of num_samples points of the trajectory; for the samples of the gate extension, the first and last trajectory points are repeated.

docs.title: Sequence calculation
docs.text:
A Pulseq sequence [2] is a list of blocks, each containing at most one RF event, one event per gradient axis, one ADC event and optional labels. The SequenceProvider, a subclass of the PyPulseq Sequence [3], calculates the sample-wise replay buffer of the transmit card from this description. The calculation is performed by AcquisitionControl.set_sequence before the acquisition starts and returns an UnrolledSequence.

docs.title: Replay buffer
docs.text:
The transmit card outputs one frame per sampling interval \(\Delta t = 1/f_\text{s}\), e.g. every 50 ns at a sampling rate of \(f_\text{s} = 20\) MHz. A frame consists of one 16-bit sample per channel. The replay buffer UnrolledSequence.seq is an int16 array that contains all frames of the sequence one after the other, as required by the FIFO mode of the transmit card. Each frame occupies 4 × 16 bit = 8 bytes, so one second of sequence at 20 MHz requires 160 MB.

---
config:
  packet:
    bitsPerRow: 64
    bitWidth: 12
---
packet-beta
title One frame: 4 samples × 16 bit = 8 bytes
0-15: "ch0: RF"
16-31: "ch1: gradient + gate"
32-47: "ch2: gradient + ref."
48-63: "ch3: gradient + unblank."

Channel 0 carries the RF waveform with the full 16-bit resolution (two's complement). Channels 1–3 carry a gradient waveform in bits 0–14 and a digital control signal in bit 15. To free bit 15, each int16 gradient sample is reinterpreted as uint16 and shifted right by one bit: bits 1–15 move to bits 0–14, and only the least significant bit is discarded. Bits 0–14 thus hold a 15-bit two's complement value, with the sign bit in bit 14 and the value bits in bits 0–13. The full scale is unchanged; the resolution is reduced by one bit. The digital signal is then set in bit 15 by a bitwise OR.

---
config:
  packet:
    bitsPerRow: 16
---
packet-beta
title Sample of channels 1–3
0-13: "gradient value bits"
14: "±"
15: "D"
Analog channel Bit 15 Digital output Description 1 ADC gate X1 Gate is high during an ADC event 2 Phase reference X2 Square wave at a fixed frequency at the start of each ADC gate 3 RF unblanking X3 Unblanking is high from the RF dead time before each RF pulse until its end

The transmit card converts bits 0–14 of channels 1–3 to the analog gradient output and routes bit 15 to its digital lines X1–X3 (see Inputs and outputs). Embedding the control signals in the waveform guarantees sample-exact synchronization of RF, gradients, ADC gate and unblanking.

docs.title: Block events
docs.text:
Each event of a block is translated into a waveform in two steps: its timing is placed on the frame raster, and its amplitude is scaled to the int16 range of the output channel.

All times of the PyPulseq sequence are converted to whole numbers of frames, i.e. a time \(t\) corresponds to \(\operatorname{round}(t \cdot f_\text{s})\) frames. Each block starts where the previous block ends, and each event starts at the block start plus its delay. The sum of all block durations must match the total duration of the sequence on the frame raster, otherwise an error is raised. This is the case if all block durations are integer multiples of \(\Delta t\), e.g. with block_duration_raster = 1 µs at 20 MHz.

The diagram shows the timing of an RF event with the attribute names of the PyPulseq RF event; the widths are not to scale.

  • RF pulse: starts delay after the block start, but not before dead_time, and lasts shape_dur. It must end within its block.
  • Unblanking: starts dead_time before the RF pulse and ends with it.
  • Ring-down: ringdown_time is not part of the waveform; it is covered by the remaining block duration.

Amplitude scaling. The complex PyPulseq envelope \(A(t)\) in Hz is resampled to the frame raster (FFT-based), modulated at the Larmor frequency \(f_0\) plus the frequency offset \(\Delta f\) of the event, and scaled to the int16 range:

\[ s(t) = 32767 \cdot \frac{\alpha_{B_1}\, \kappa_\text{RF}}{U_\text{RF,max}} \cdot \operatorname{Re}\left\{ A(t)\, e^{j\varphi}\, e^{j 2\pi (f_0 + \Delta f)\, t} \right\} \]

The time \(t\) starts at zero at the beginning of each pulse, so the phase of a pulse does not depend on its position in the sequence. The result is truncated to int16. An RF amplitude above the output limit raises an error. If an RF gain lookup table is configured (rf_gain_lut_path), it is applied to the int16 samples to linearize the RF power amplifier.

Amplitude scaling. The gradient amplitude \(G\) in Hz/m is converted to the output voltage \(U\) of the channel and scaled to the int16 range:

\[ q = 32767 \cdot \frac{U}{U_\text{max}}, \qquad U = \frac{s_\text{FoV}\, G}{\gamma\, g\, \eta} \]

\(U\) results in V; \(U_\text{max}\) is converted to the same unit. The result is truncated to int16 and stored with 15 bits (see Replay buffer). A gradient amplitude above the output limit raises an error.

The diagram shows the attribute names of the PyPulseq ADC event; the widths are not to scale. The ADC samples start delay after the block start and last num_samples × dwell:

  • ADC gate: extended on both sides by dead_time, rounded down to a whole number of dwell times. The receive data of the extension are discarded after processing.
  • Phase reference: 1.095 MHz square wave during the first 1000 frames of the gate (50 µs at 20 MHz), or the whole gate if it is shorter.

For each ADC event, an RxData template is created. It contains the sample counts, dwell times, frequency and phase offsets of the event, and the PyPulseq labels set since the previous ADC event. The templates are filled with data during the acquisition (see Postprocessing).
